claim: NCERT defines a volcano as a place where gases, ashes and/or molten rock (lava) escape to the ground; USGS adds that the word also means the vent itself and usually a cone built around it
value: volcano = vent + (usually) cone built from its own products
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: USGS section 'The Nature of Volcanoes'.

claim: Definition of 'active volcano' differs: NCERT says active if material is being or was released in the recent past; USGS (1997) says active means erupted at least once in recorded history. No single official definition was read
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Teach as two working definitions. The Smithsonian GVP uses a Holocene test but its page is BLOCKED (see C-block in dossier).

claim: Magma is molten rock below the surface; it is called lava only after it erupts. NCERT p.23 says material already moving toward the crust is called lava, which is looser than USGS
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
page_or_section: section 'The Nature of Volcanoes'; also NCERT Cl.XI Ch3 printed p.23
second_source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Teach the USGS rule. NCERT sentence on p.23: 'Once it starts moving towards the crust or it reaches the surface, it is referred to as lava.'

claim: NCERT lists the material that reaches the ground: lava flows, pyroclastic debris, volcanic bombs, ash and dust, and gases such as nitrogen compounds, sulphur compounds and small amounts of chlorine, hydrogen and argon
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: USGS names lava, bombs, ash flows and tephra (airborne ash and dust) as what builds a volcano. This list is what UPSC 2024 Q3 tests (V006).

claim: USGS says more than 90% of the gas from volcanoes is water vapour; other common gases are carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen and fluorine. Water vapour and carbon dioxide are missing from NCERT's list, and nitrogen compounds are not in USGS's list
source: USGS Fact Sheet 002-97 'What Are Volcano Hazards?' (revised March 2008; superseded by FS 2018-3075)
second_source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: FS 002-97 is marked superseded by FS 2018-3075; only its landing page was read (full text not opened). Exam answer follows NCERT; science answer follows USGS. Show the disagreement.

claim: UPSC Prelims 2024 GS I Q3 asked: of pyroclastic debris, ash and dust, nitrogen compounds and sulphur compounds, how many are products of volcanic eruptions (options: one, two, three, all four). NCERT p.23 lists all four, so the NCERT-based answer is (d) all four
source: UPSC Civil Services (Preliminary) Examination 2024, General Studies Paper I (OCR of page 3)
page_or_section: Q3 on paper page 3 (OCR); also NCERT Cl.XI Ch3 printed p.23
second_source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Question wording CONFIRMED from the UPSC paper (OCR of an image-only PDF). The answer is OUR inference from NCERT; UPSC's official answer key was not read (see open items).

claim: Tephra is the name for rock fragments blasted out; bombs are the largest and usually land within about 2 miles of the vent, while ash (finer than about 0.1 inch) rises high and travels farthest
source: USGS Fact Sheet 002-97 'What Are Volcano Hazards?' (revised March 2008; superseded by FS 2018-3075)
note: Single source. Size classes in metric units not given in the page.

claim: Pyroclastic flows are fast avalanches of hot ash, rock fragments and gas down a volcano's side; USGS says they can be as hot as 1,500 degrees Fahrenheit (about 800 C, our conversion)
source: USGS Fact Sheet 002-97 'What Are Volcano Hazards?' (revised March 2008; superseded by FS 2018-3075)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Pele 1902 and Pinatubo are examples (V062, V060). USGS text 1997 also names 'nuees ardentes' with plinian eruptions.

claim: Explosive or gentle depends on the lava: thin fluid lava lets gas escape quietly; thick pasty (viscous) lava traps gas until it bursts out. USGS compares it to shaking a fizzy drink and removing your thumb. This is an analogy, and it stops being true because magma gas comes out of the melt as pressure falls, not from shaking
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
second_source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth', Plate tectonics and people (natural hazards)
note: Analogy is USGS's own; the 'where it stops being true' sentence is OURS (inference). This Dynamic Earth repeats the bottle image for subduction volcanoes.

claim: Violent gas release can make pumice, a rock froth so full of bubbles that some floats on water
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Fun fact. One source: S4 needs a second source before it goes on screen.

claim: NCERT classifies volcanoes by the nature of the eruption and the form built: shield, composite, caldera, flood basalt province and mid-ocean ridge volcanoes. USGS groups cone-building volcanoes into four kinds (cinder cone, composite, shield, lava dome) and treats calderas as collapse depressions and flood basalts as lava plateaus
value: NCERT 5 types; USGS 4 cone kinds + calderas + plateaus
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes', Principal Types of Volcanoes page
note: Two valid classifications. Exam: use NCERT's five; add USGS's cinder cone and lava dome as extras.

claim: Shield volcanoes are broad and gently sloping because they are built from very runny basalt lava; NCERT names the Hawaiian volcanoes as the famous examples and says they turn explosive only if water gets into the vent. USGS calls Mauna Loa the largest shield volcano and the world's largest active volcano, rising 13,677 feet above sea level
value: Mauna Loa 13,677 ft above sea level (1997)
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
page_or_section: section 'Shield volcanoes'; also NCERT Cl.XI Ch3 printed p.23
second_source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT p.23-24. Mauna Loa erupted 27 Nov to 10 Dec 2022 per USGS HVO (seen only as a search snippet; usgs.gov page not read). Keep recent eruptions out of core teaching.

claim: Composite volcanoes erupt cooler, stickier lava with ash, so they build steep cones of alternating layers and often explode; USGS names Mount Fuji and Cotopaxi (Ecuador) among them and calls them stratovolcanoes
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: USGS section 'Composite volcanoes'. This Dynamic Earth: subduction-zone volcanoes like St Helens and Pinatubo are composite cones.

claim: A caldera is a big collapse depression left when a volcano empties its magma chamber and the top falls in; NCERT treats it as a volcano type, USGS as a depression, with Crater Lake (Oregon) formed about 6,800 years ago as the example and circular calderas from 1 to 15 miles across and elongated ones up to 60 miles long
value: caldera = collapse; Crater Lake ~6,800 years ago
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: NCERT says the magma chamber is 'huge' and 'in close vicinity'.

claim: A cinder cone is the simplest volcano, built from cinders thrown out of one vent; Paricutin in Mexico began in 1943 on a farm and grew to about 1,200 feet in 9 years of activity
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes', Principal Types of Volcanoes page
second_source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT p.23 shows a cinder cone figure and p.24 says shield vents can throw up cinder cones. Fun fact; one source for the numbers.

claim: Flood basalt provinces are made of very fluid lava that spreads for long distances in many flows; NCERT says flows can exceed 50 m thick and run for hundreds of km. USGS says lava plateaus form when basalt pours quietly from long fissures, as in Iceland, Washington, Oregon and Idaho
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: NCERT figure '50 m' and 'hundreds of km' are NCERT's own; USGS gives Columbia/Snake River flows 'more than a mile' total thickness.

claim: NCERT says the mid-ocean ridge system is more than 70,000 km long; NOAA Ocean Exploration gives nearly 65,000 km (40,390 miles) and USGS 'This Dynamic Earth' gives more than 50,000 km
value: NCERT >70,000 km; NOAA ~65,000 km; USGS TDE >50,000 km
source: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 'What is a mid-ocean ridge?'
page_or_section: section 'What is a mid-ocean ridge?'; also NCERT Cl.XI Ch3 printed p.24
second_source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth', Developing the theory of plate tectonics (and Plate tectonics and people)
note: Three publishers, three figures: NCERT p.24 'more than 70,000 km'; NOAA 'nearly 65,000 km'; USGS This Dynamic Earth 'more than 50,000 km' (saved dynamic_developing.txt lines 56-57 and 120; dynamic_tectonics.txt line 306). Name the source with the figure; do not teach one 'correct' length or use a spot-the-mistake on 70,000. [Audit 3 Nov 2026: the earlier note that USGS gives 65,000 km was wrong; no saved USGS text says it.]

claim: About three quarters of all lava erupted on Earth comes out unseen under the ocean, mostly at the spreading centres such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and East Pacific Rise
source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth', Plate tectonics and people (natural hazards)
second_source: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 'What is a mid-ocean ridge?'
note: NOAA confirms ridges are divergent boundaries with basalt eruptions but does not give the 75% figure. One source for the number.

claim: Lava that cools at the surface makes volcanic rocks; magma that cools underground makes plutonic (intrusive) rocks, which are coarser grained because they cool slowly. NCERT names the underground shapes 'intrusive forms'
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: USGS: slow cooling gives 'coarser grained, nearly completely crystalline' rocks; granitic rocks of Yosemite are exhumed examples.

claim: Batholith: a huge granitic body that cooled deep in the crust as the cooled part of a magma chamber; it shows at the surface only after erosion (denudation) removes the rock above. NCERT is the only source for these intrusive-form definitions
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: No publisher definition was read (the usgs.gov glossary is behind a bot check). USGS GIP supports the idea that granite is exposed by erosion (V019).

claim: Laccolith: a dome-shaped intrusion with a level base fed through a pipe-like conduit; NCERT calls it a deep version of a surface volcanic dome. Lapolith is a saucer-shaped (concave) body, phacolith a wavy body at the base of a syncline or crest of an anticline, a sill is thick and near-horizontal, a sheet is thin and near-horizontal
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT spells it 'lacolith'. NCERT-only; marked for expert review (R1).

claim: NCERT says the domal granite hills of the Karnataka plateau, now mostly exfoliated, are examples of laccoliths or batholiths
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: No publisher or paper on these hills was read. Keep off screen or say 'NCERT gives this example'. OPEN ITEMS 2026-11-10: still UNVERIFIED. A Crossref search for a paper or Geological Survey of India text on the Karnataka domal hills returned nothing relevant; no official source read. Say 'NCERT gives this example' or keep off screen.

claim: A dyke forms when magma fills cracks and fissures and hardens almost vertically as a wall-like body; NCERT says dykes are the commonest intrusive form in western Maharashtra and fed the Deccan Traps. USGS says lava hardened in fissures forms dikes, which strengthen a composite cone, and erosion can leave a plug-and-dike skeleton behind
value: dyke = vertical wall of hardened magma
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Srivastava et al. 2020 date mafic dykes in eastern India (Damodar valley) at about 70.5 to 65.5 Ma and link them to the Reunion plume, so dykes outside western Maharashtra also belong to the Deccan story (V053).

claim: Most active volcanoes sit at or near plate boundaries; some form in plate interiors over hotspots. NCERT Grade 9 (2026) says most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries, especially around the Pacific (Ring of Fire)
source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 1, Ch2 Shaping of the Earth's Surface (First ed. June 2026)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: USGS text 1997 section 'Plate-Tectonics Theory'.

claim: Two boundary recipes: where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate the oceanic plate sinks, giving volcanoes and earthquakes (convergent); where plates move apart, magma rises and makes new crust, as at mid-ocean ridges (divergent). USGS adds that most above-sea volcanoes are near convergent boundaries
value: convergent = subduction volcanoes; divergent = ridge volcanoes
source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 1, Ch2 Shaping of the Earth's Surface (First ed. June 2026)
second_source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth', Plate tectonics and people (natural hazards)
note: NCERT Grade 9 does not mention water in the subduction melting recipe, so do not teach that step from NCERT; USGS This Dynamic Earth was read only for the places above.

claim: The Ring of Fire is the belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific rim; USGS says more than half of the world's active volcanoes encircle the Pacific and it is the most seismically and volcanically active zone in the world. NCERT Class XI says the Pacific rim is called the rim of fire because of its active volcanoes
value: more than half of active volcanoes (USGS 1997)
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch4 Distribution of Oceans and Continents (Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Do not use '75% of volcanoes' or '90% of earthquakes': not found at an allowed source in this build.

claim: Hawaii shows a hotspot: the islands formed over 3,200 km from the nearest plate boundary as the Pacific plate moved over a fixed hot region in the mantle (J. Tuzo Wilson's idea of 1963); older islands lie farther along the chain, with Kauai's oldest rocks about 5.5 million years old
source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth', Hotspots
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: USGS text 1997 also says Hawaii is the best example of an intra-plate chain.

claim: Deccan Traps have been linked to a hotspot track running from the Deccan through the Chagos-Laccadive ridge to Reunion Island, where lava is still erupting; Sen notes there is considerable debate about whether such plumes rise from the core-mantle boundary
value: Deccan to Reunion hotspot track (standard model)
source: Sen G. (2001) Generation of Deccan Trap magmas, J. Earth Syst. Sci. 110:409-431
page_or_section: Sen PDF p.6 (section 2.1); also Srivastava 2020 pdf p.1
second_source: Srivastava, Wang, Shi (2020) Reunion plume induced magmatic pulses of the Deccan LIP, eastern India, J. Earth Syst. Sci. 129:96
note: Standard model, not unanimous. Srivastava et al. 2020 say mafic dykes are 'supposedly related to the Reunion mantle plume'. An IIT Bombay overview challenging the plume model appeared only in a search snippet and was not read.

claim: Volcanoes and earthquakes cluster in the same belts because both answer to the same plate movements; NCERT notes 'volcanic earthquakes' occur only in areas of active volcanoes. A 2021 study found earthquakes near Barren Island were 3.54 times more frequent in 1990-2020 than 1950-1989, which the authors infer signifies seismicity-induced pressure release that may have caused decompression leading to eruptions or modulating them (their inference; they also say the earthquake swarms cluster along regional tectonic structures, not at the volcano)
value: 3.54x more frequent (authors' inference: quakes may have led to or modulated eruptions)
source: Gunda, Ray, Chauhan, Chauhan, Balaji (2021) Barren Island volcanism and seismicity, J. Earth Syst. Sci. 130:162
page_or_section: PDF p.1 (Abstract); also NCERT Cl.XI Ch3 printed p.20
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Correlation, not proven cause. USGS text 1997: volcanism and seismic activity 'respond to the same dynamic Earth forces'. NCERT p.20 for volcanic earthquakes (heading 'Earthquake' is GEO-03's).

claim: NCERT says the energy behind endogenic processes is mostly generated by radioactivity, rotational and tidal friction, and primordial heat. Davies and Davies (2010) put Earth's surface heat loss at 47 +/- 2 TW and say the mantle share (24-38 TW) comes from heat generation in the mantle and the planet's secular cooling, 'plus minor contributions from other sources'; they name no tidal or rotational heating.
value: 47 +/- 2 TW surface heat; bulk silicate Earth radiogenic heat about 20 TW
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch5 Geomorphic Processes (Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: Davies J.H. and Davies D.R. (2010) Earth's surface heat flux, Solid Earth 1:5-24 (Copernicus, peer reviewed), Section 'Discussion' p.~19
note: Davies and Davies (2010) give the total heat Earth loses but not this breakdown; they mention mantle radioactive heating and a primordial magma ocean remnant only in passing. OPEN ITEMS 2026-11-10: read in sources/v030/davies2010.txt (line ~2505-2520). Fix: teach 'radioactive decay and the Earth's leftover (primordial) heat' as the big two; tidal and rotational friction are not named by this paper, and no ranking of shares by NCERT is supported. A text search of the paper finds no mention of tides. This is absence in one paper, not proof; keep tidal/rotational friction as 'NCERT lists it'.

claim: Earth loses about 47 terawatts of heat through its surface, the best estimate of Davies and Davies (2010), who give 47 plus or minus 2 TW
source: Davies J.H. and Davies D.R. (2010) Earth's surface heat flux, Solid Earth 1:5-24
note: One peer-reviewed estimate; later estimates not searched. Good 'how much heat leaks out' fact; comparison to human power use is not sourced.

claim: NCERT names volcanism, with diastrophism, as an endogenic (inside-driven) geomorphic process; volcanism is movement of magma onto or toward the surface plus the making of intrusive and extrusive forms. Diastrophism covers orogeny, epeirogeny, earthquakes and plate movement. NCERT p.38-39 points back to 'igneous rocks in the preceding chapter', a chapter (Minerals and Rocks) dropped in the 2022 rationalisation
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch5 Geomorphic Processes (Reprint 2026-27)
note: Stale cross-reference confirmed in BookletClass11.txt (Chapter 5 Minerals and Rocks, old pp.40-44, full chapter deleted).

claim: NCERT says endogenic forces are mainly land-building and exogenic processes (weathering, mass movement, erosion, deposition) are mainly land-wearing; USGS shows the same in a volcano's life: once a composite cone goes dormant, erosion strips it until only the hard plug and dike remain
value: volcano builds; weather and rivers wear
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch5 Geomorphic Processes (Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Links volcano episode to GEO-05 (rivers) and weathering. Heading 'Exogenic Processes' is otherwise not this episode's.

claim: Crust: NCERT gives mean thickness 5 km (oceanic) and about 30 km (continental), up to 70 km in the Himalayan region; USGS gives about 5 km under oceans, 30 km average on continents and up to 100 km under big ranges such as the Alps
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth' (Kious and Tilling), Inside the Earth
note: Different maxima (70 km Himalaya v 100 km big ranges) are two different statements, not a contradiction.

claim: Mantle: runs from the Moho down to 2,900 km; USGS describes it as hot, dense semi-solid rock about 2,900 km thick. NCERT's lower mantle 'is in solid state'
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth' (Kious and Tilling), Inside the Earth
note: 'Semi-solid' (USGS) v 'solid' (NCERT) is a wording difference; teach 'solid rock that flows very slowly' only if a source is added.

claim: NCERT calls the asthenosphere (upper mantle, 'weak' zone, said to extend to about 400 km) the main source of magma. USGS describes magma forming by local melting in the upper mantle and, on continents, also in the crust. The 400 km depth and the 'main source' wording were not confirmed at any publisher
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Teach 'magma forms in the hot upper mantle' (supported); keep '400 km' off screen unless a publisher is read. OPEN ITEMS 2026-11-10: still UNVERIFIED. USGS This Dynamic Earth page (sources/v036/dyn_inside.txt) names the asthenosphere as the weak mobile zone below the lithosphere but gives no depth, and USGS pages on the VHP site returned 403. No publisher read for '400 km' or 'main source of magma'.

claim: Lithosphere: NCERT says it is the crust plus the uppermost mantle, 10 to 200 km thick; USGS says the plates average about 50 miles (about 80 km) thick
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Volcanoes' (Tilling, 1997 text), full text
note: Different statements (range v average). Conversion miles to km is ours.

claim: Core: boundary at 2,900 km depth; outer core liquid, inner core solid, mostly nickel and iron (NCERT 'nife'). USGS gives a 2,200 km thick liquid outer core, a 1,250 km solid inner core and an iron-nickel alloy
value: outer liquid 2,200 km; inner solid 1,250 km
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth' (Kious and Tilling), Inside the Earth
note: Light elements in the core are not in either source.

claim: Direct sources: NCERT says the deepest drill at Kola is 'in Arctic Ocean' and about 12 km deep; it also names volcanic eruptions as a direct source (magma reaches labs, though its source depth is hard to tell). The Kola Superdeep Borehole is on land on Russia's Kola Peninsula, 10 km south-west of Zapolyarny, and reached 12,262 m in 1990
source: Skuf'in P.K. (2021) Anniversary of the commencement of the SG-3 Kola superdeep borehole drilling, Nexo Scientific Journal 34(4):1477-1489, doi 10.5377/nexo.v34i04.12693
page_or_section: PDF p.1 (Abstract) and p.3 (location); also NCERT Cl.XI Ch3 printed p.18
second_source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT p.18 wording is wrong about the sea. Depth '12 km' is right. Rest of Direct Sources (mines, drilling projects) is GEO-01's.

claim: At about 12 km depth Kola recorded temperatures up to 220 C, which caused repeated accidents and breakage during drilling
source: Skuf'in P.K. (2021) Anniversary of the commencement of the SG-3 Kola superdeep borehole drilling, Nexo Scientific Journal 34(4):1477-1489, doi 10.5377/nexo.v34i04.12693
note: Fun fact on how hot depth is. One source (Russian geologist's review). [Audit: the same paper also reports a measured 212 C at 12 km and 180 C at about 10 km; 'up to 220 C' is its figure for the bottomhole.]

claim: NCERT p.18 names 'Deep Ocean Drilling Project' and 'Integrated Ocean Drilling Project'. Sources read give: the Integrated Ocean Drilling Program (2003-2013; a Program, not a Project), the International Ocean Discovery Program (from 2013), and IODP3, the International Ocean Drilling Programme, starting January 2025. What 'Deep Ocean Drilling Project' refers to (earlier DSDP/ODP names) was not read at any saved source: UNVERIFIED
source: ECORD, news headlines (IODP3 start announcement, 12 March 2024)
page_or_section: headline of 12 March 2024; also NCERT Cl.XI Ch3 printed p.18
second_source: NCPOR/IODP India, 'IODP - Background and History'
note: [Audit 3 Nov 2026: removed DSDP/ODP names from the 'real sequence' because no saved source gives them.] India's NCPOR page gives the 2013-2023 end year; ECORD says the Discovery Program ends 2024. Current drilling status after Jan 2025 not read. LIVING fact.

claim: Indirect evidence: NCERT says temperature, pressure and density all rise with depth, and gravity anomalies, magnetic surveys, meteorites and seismic activity add information; USGS also says temperature and pressure inside Earth increase with depth
value: T, P, density rise with depth
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS 'This Dynamic Earth' (Kious and Tilling), Inside the Earth
note: Rest of Indirect Sources belongs to GEO-01.

claim: Barren Island, in the Andaman Sea, is the only active volcano in India: NCERT Class XI says so, and a peer-reviewed study (Sheth et al. 2009) says the same for 'Indian territory'
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch2 Structure and Physiography (Rev. ed. Feb 2022, reprint 2026-27)
page_or_section: p.15 (Andaman and Nicobar Islands); also Sheth 2009 pdf p.1
second_source: Sheth, Ray, Bhutani, Kumar, Smitha (2009) Volcanology and eruptive styles of Barren Island, Bulletin of Volcanology, doi 10.1007/s00445-009-0280-z
note: 'Only active' is a status at publication dates. Check the live position before any script (see V047).

claim: Barren Island lies in the Andaman Sea about 70 km east of the Andaman chain and is the northernmost active volcano of the Indonesian arc; the Indian plate subducts along the Andaman Trench
source: Sheth, Ray, Bhutani, Kumar, Smitha (2009) Volcanology and eruptive styles of Barren Island, Bulletin of Volcanology, doi 10.1007/s00445-009-0280-z
second_source: Gunda, Ray, Chauhan, Chauhan, Balaji (2021) Barren Island volcanism and seismicity, J. Earth Syst. Sci. 130:162
note: Gives the plate-boundary reason an Indian volcano exists.

claim: Barren Island's recorded eruptions: sketches show the volcano existed by 1787; 'historic' eruptions 1787-1832; recent eruptions 1991, 1994-95 and 2005-06 (and one begun 2008, tephra only). A 2021 paper says the volcano erupted vigorously again from 2018 after a 13-year gap, last active 2004-2005
source: Sheth, Ray, Bhutani, Kumar, Smitha (2009) Volcanology and eruptive styles of Barren Island, Bulletin of Volcanology, doi 10.1007/s00445-009-0280-z
page_or_section: PDF p.1 (Abstract and Introduction); also Gunda 2021 pdf p.1
